title: Quantum Systems upgrades long-range Reliant unmanned aircraft system
summary: The latest generation of Reliant features a hybrid-electric power unit and increases the system's payload capacity to up to nine kilograms, enabling a broader range of missions.
body_text: Quantum Systems is announcing major upgrades to its long-range intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance (ISR) system, Reliant. Following Quantum Systems’ policy of continuous development and research and development (R&D), the new features significantly expand Reliant’s mission flexibility while maintaining the ease of deployment and low logistical footprint that define Quantum Systems’ platforms. The latest generation of Reliant features a hybrid-electric power unit and increases the system’s payload capacity to up to nine kilograms, enabling a much broader range of missions. Depending on operational requirements, Reliant can now carry electro-optical sensors, laser-target designators, synthetic aperture radar (SAR), SIGINT and electronic warfare payloads, as well as SATCOM, relay and other mission-specific capabilities. Despite its expanded capabilities, Reliant maintains its minimal logistical footprint with easy-packaging options and operations enablement for assembly by a two-person team and operations by a single operator. The hybrid-electric VTOL platform requires only a 10 × 10 meter launch and recovery area, making it independent of start and recovery infrastructure and suitable for ship-based operations. Beyond the platform itself, Reliant is fully integrated into the MOSAIC UXS software platform, making it interoperable with other unmanned systems in multi-domain operations. Together with operator workstations, training, sustainment and lifecycle support, Quantum Systems delivers a complete long-range unmanned capability rather than a standalone aircraft. Reliant also completes Quantum Systems’ Family of Aerial Systems, complementing the short-range Twister and the mid-range Vector AI platforms. Quantum Systems UAS solutions are already in service with a range of NATO and allied armed forces, notably with the German Armed Forces and the Armed Forces of Ukraine. Reliant is built around a secure European supply chain and supported by Quantum Systems’ growing industrial base, providing customers with a system without any Chinese components or ITAR restrictions. “Reliant’s upgrades are the result of continuous feedback from military users and partners, and our answer to enhance long-range capabilities for NATO, Europe and our allies,” said Martin Karkour, chief revenue officer at Quantum Systems. “We can now offer a truly unique capability, with a minimal logistical footprint, payload superpower and impressive range and endurance— completely built on a resilient supply chain. We are very proud of that.” This press release was prepared and distributed by Quantum Systems.

title: OPAL Fuels to Supply Municipal Refuse Fleet with Renewable Natural Gas Across California’s Central Valley
summary: Agreement includes CNG fueling station upgrades and has the capacity to dispense 4 million GGE of low-carbon fuel over the next decade, expanding access for the growing agricultural hub WHITE PLAINS, N.Y. --(BUSINESS WIRE)--Jul. 30, 2026-- OPAL Fuels (Nasdaq: OPAL), a leader in the production,
body_text: PDF Version Agreement includes CNG fueling station upgrades and has the capacity to dispense 4 million GGE of low-carbon fuel over the next decade, expanding access for the growing agricultural hub WHITE PLAINS, N.Y.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Jul. 30, 2026-- OPAL Fuels (Nasdaq: OPAL), a leader in the production, marketing, and distribution of renewable and compressed natural gas (RNG and CNG) used as a transportation fuel for heavy duty trucking, today announced that it is building a new fueling station in the City of Dinuba, and will own and maintain the station through a long-term agreement with the City and its partners that provide municipal services. Most immediately, the station will supply CNG to the refuse collection fleet of Peña’s Disposal Service, the City’s contracted refuse services provider, as well as other CNG vehicles serving Dinuba and the surrounding areas, one of California’s most productive agricultural regions. As part of the long-term agreement, the new station will also dispense RNG, a carbon-negative to low-carbon fuel derived from organic waste sources such as landfills, dairy waste, and wastewater treatment plants, to power the refuse trucks that serve the community daily. The station is expected to be open to the public, giving the City of Dinuba and other local fleet operators access to renewable fuel. “We are proud to invest in the City of Dinuba’s fueling infrastructure and help Peña’s Disposal Service deliver essential services more sustainably,” said Adam Comora, Co-Chief Executive Officer of OPAL Fuels. “With RNG consistently beating diesel on cost while also reducing emissions, this partnership benefits both the community and the environment.” Once operational, the station is projected to displace approximately 400,000 gallons of diesel annually. About OPAL Fuels OPAL Fuels (Nasdaq: OPAL) is a leader in the capture and conversion of biogas into low carbon intensity RNG and renewable electricity. OPAL Fuels is also a leader in the marketing and distribution of RNG to heavy duty trucking and other hard to decarbonize industrial sectors. For additional information, and to learn more about OPAL Fuels and how it is leading the effort to capture North America’s harmful methane emissions and decarbonize the economy, please visit www.opalfuels.com . title: Inside Aurora’s Photonic Engine: Engineering Lidar for Automotive Scale

body_text: To move our FMCW lidar from discrete optics to an automotive-grade photonic engine built for scale, Aurora has assembled a team with deep expertise in integrated photonics, compound semiconductor design, and precision optical manufacturing. This blog was written by three members of that team: James Ferrara , Phillip Sandborn , and Parth Panchal . Imagine building a sensor that manipulates light at the nanometer scale (70,000 times narrower than a human hair) while detecting objects a kilometer away. It has to do that while surviving road vibration, temperature extremes, and the reliability standards of the automotive industry, in a package small enough to fit in the palm of your hand. Aurora’s Firstlight LiDAR photonics engine These are the challenges we work on every day as part of the Aurora Lidar team. In the transition from development and testing of our lidar-on-a-chip into a product qualified for commercial operations, the demands on our sensors have sharpened. Bottom-line sensor performance still matters, but the system also has to be manufactured repeatably, qualified to automotive standards, and built in much larger volumes. At Aurora, we’ve developed high-performance lidar sensors over many years, and the work ahead is just as significant. Our near-term goal is to put thousands of self-driving trucks on the road, and our photonic engine is central to that mission. How the Aurora Driver sees the road The Aurora Driver perceives its environment through a combination of lidar, radar, and cameras, each playing a crucial role in building a comprehensive picture of the road ahead. For lidar, the Aurora Driver uses an FMCW (Frequency-Modulated Continuous-Wave) approach. Rather than firing short pulses and timing their return (the way a bat uses echolocation), FMCW lidar sends out a continuous beam whose frequency changes in a known pattern, then mixes the return signal with a local reference beam. That approach proves immensely valuable when driving an 80,000 pound robot at highway speeds. Because moving objects impose a doppler shift on the return light, every point in the point cloud carries its own instantaneous velocity. The Aurora Driver can distinguish a stopped vehicle from one merging across a lane without waiting to compare multiple returns to determine the object’s velocity. And because the receiver only responds to light that matches the emitted frequency and timing, sunlight and other vehicles' lidar read as noise rather than as phantom objects. High-density point cloud from Aurora’s lidar test range in Bozeman, MT The next generation of our FirstLight lidar reaches up to one kilometer of range, roughly double that of the closest FMCW competitor. At typical highway speeds, this can give the Aurora Driver more than 34 seconds to react to future scenarios accordingly. How we got here The photonic engine did not arrive in one breakthrough. It is the product of years of acquired expertise and iteration. The FMCW lidar approach is core to our self-driving truck strategy. The architecture and signal-processing depth that came with the acquisition of Blackmore in 2019 is what first let us train and test Aurora Driver-powered trucks on public highways, fulfilling the company mission of deploying self-driving technology safely and quickly. However, FMCW implemented with discrete optics meant bulky assemblies of fiber, lasers, and transceivers, workable for a test fleet but expensive and likely impractical for a real production fleet. The silicon photonics and packaging expertise of the OURS team, acquired in 2021, gave us a path to condense those discrete parts onto chips. By 2023 we had demonstrated the individual optical functions working in chip form. Today, we have iterated over multiple generations of design and fabrication, refining both the photonic building blocks and the packaging that holds them together. Photonic integration is what makes it possible to now deploy a high-performance lidar sensor at commercial scale. Owning the lidar stack The atomically thin epitaxial layers of our lasers and optical amplifiers, the low-loss silicon-nitride waveguides, the high-responsivity photodiodes, even the microoptical couplers that route light in and out of the engine: each of these gives us multiple opportunities to optimize the sensor for performance, manufacturing, testing, and validation against strict automotive qualification standards. We understand exactly how our hardware behaves across operating conditions, iterate on chip designs quickly guided by performance data across large datasets, and build toward automotive qualification with full visibility into every layer of the stack. Owning the design, the IP, the process know-how, and the manufacturing transfer is what allows us to build a high-performance lidar sensor at the volume commercial deployment requires. What the photonic engine does Our photonic engine is a multi-chip module that consolidates the core optical functions required for lidar into a single compact assembly: light generation, amplification, modulation, transmission, and detection. Two device families do most of the work. Silicon photonic integrated circuits route and manipulate light within the system. Our latest generation delivers more than 10% lower on-chip optical loss than the prior generation, and our custom-designed photodiode achieves 25% higher sensitivity than the comparable foundry library components. After a kilometer, the returning light is extraordinarily faint, and detection comes down to whether enough photons clear the noise floor. Every fraction of a decibel of loss removed inside the module, and every bit of sensitivity added at the detector, adds up to photons that make the difference between seeing an object or not. Light is generated and amplified by compound semiconductor (III-V) devices: a semiconductor laser source and custom semiconductor optical amplifiers, or SOAs. The silicon photonics route modulates and detects light; the III-V components generate and boost the light. We developed our amplifiers in-house in under two years, and co-designed them with the silicon photonic chips from the start. This lets us move past basic datasheet comparison for vendor-produced parts and towards a perfectly tuned system. This “custom-design” philosophy is core to how we hit loss and efficiency targets that the system requires. The system is also fiber-free. Fiber connectors in vehicle environments accumulate fatigue damage from continuous vibration. Over hundreds of thousands of miles, that mechanical stress degrades optical coupling and introduces failure modes that are difficult to predict or inspect. Our design routes light through integrated photonics and precision-engineered optical interfaces instead, eliminating that failure mechanism and giving us a more compact, qualification-friendly package. The hardest part: moving light between chips A core capability to achieve the “perfectly-tuned” system for reliable automotive conditions is our ability to perform active alignment of microlenses between chips during the assembly process. Moving light reliably between multiple chips inside a compact package requires sub-micron alignment tolerances, maintained under vibration, thermal cycling, and years of service life on a commercial truck. The process that achieves this has to be repeatable at manufacturing scale. In a lab, you can take your time with each alignment. On a production line, you don’t have that luxury. The Aurora photonic engine in action: light is emitted and received by the module at the heart of our Firstlight system (photo captured with an infrared-sensitive filter with a long exposure) So we align lens couplers actively. As each lens is placed, we send light through our chips and monitor the coupled optical power in real time, minutely adjusting the lens position until the signal peaks, then fixing it there. Running that with automated sensor-driven feedback on every optical path is what turns laboratory-grade coupling into a repeatable manufacturing step. This active-alignment know-how and expertise has been developed over several years, and is essential to bringing the photonics engine to production. Building for production Performance is necessary but not sufficient for an automotive-grade system. The harder bar is proving the part can be built the same way, to the same spec, every time, at volume. Automotive supply chains run on frameworks like PPAP (Production Part Approval Process), which require documented evidence of design validation, process control, and measurement system capability before a part is approved for production. It is how an OEM gains confidence that a supplier can deliver consistent quality across hundreds of thousands of units, not just one good prototype. We have designed the photonic engine toward that bar from early in the program rather than treating qualification as a final gate. In practice that means building manufacturability into the architecture, standing up internal test platforms that screen components across large statistical datasets, and tracking performance trends across design generations. It also means taking on a harder version of the problem than most photonics programs face. Because we mount bare dies and align them optically inside the package, qualifying the assembly means qualifying the process that builds it, not just dropping in parts that arrive pre-qualified. That is more work up front, and it is the right kind of work for a part that has to survive years of service on the road. What comes next The photonic engine we have today is one stage in a longer development story. The photonics industry is moving toward higher levels of integration: co-packaged optics, hybrid approaches that consolidate multiple optical functions into fewer components. Done right, that means smaller packages and lower cost without sacrificing the reliability standards automotive deployment requires. We are already exploring what that looks like for our architecture. Concretely, our next step is pulling more of these discrete optical functions onto fewer chips while leveraging the alignment precision and reliability margins we have spent years building. Integration is easy to chase if you are willing to relax the automotive constraints. We are not. This work spans nanophotonics, compound semiconductor design, precision micro-optical assembly, automotive qualification, and systems engineering at scale. Most teams spend careers in one of those domains. At Aurora, they all converge on a single problem – with real trucks moving freight on public highways depending on the answer. There are still plenty of hard problems in autonomous sensing to solve. That is what makes this work worth doing.

body_text: View All News Surf Air Mobility Receives Continued Listing Standard Notice from NYSE July 24, 2026 Surf Air Mobility continues to trade on the NYSE under ticker symbol SRFM. LOS ANGELES--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- Surf Air Mobility Inc. (NYSE: SRFM) (“Surf Air Mobility”), a leading air mobility platform, today announced that on July 24, 2026, it received notice from the New York Stock Exchange (“NYSE”) that it is not in compliance with Section 802.01C of the NYSE Listed Company Manual because the average closing price of Surf Air Mobility’s Common Stock was less than $1.00 over a consecutive 30 trading-day period. The NYSE notice has no immediate impact on the listing of Surf Air Mobility’s Common Stock, and the Common Stock will continue to be listed and trade on the NYSE, subject to Surf Air Mobility’s compliance with other NYSE continued listing standards. Surf Air Mobility plans to notify the NYSE within 10 business days that it intends to regain compliance with Rule 802.01C and cure the stock price deficiency. Surf Air Mobility can regain compliance at any time within the six-month period following receipt of the NYSE notice if on the last trading day of any calendar month during the cure period Surf Air Mobility has a closing share price of at least $1.00 and an average closing share price of at least $1.00 over the 30 trading-day period ending on the last trading day of that month. Surf Air Mobility intends to regain compliance organically. If necessary, the Company will also consider alternative means of compliance, including, but not limited to, a reverse stock split, which the Company’s shareholders approved at Surf Air Mobility's July 24, 2026 Annual Meeting of Stockholders. Shareholder approval is a risk mitigation tool and does not commit the Company to a specific course of action. Under the NYSE’s rules, if Surf Air Mobility determines that it will cure the stock price deficiency through a reverse stock split, the price condition will be deemed cured if the price promptly exceeds $1.00 per share, and the price remains above that level for at least the following 30 trading days. The notice is not anticipated to impact the ongoing business operations of Surf Air Mobility and its subsidiaries or its reporting requirements with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission. About Surf Air Mobility Surf Air Mobility is a Los Angeles-based air mobility platform. With its AI-enabled SurfOS software, Surf Air Mobility provides technology designed to support the modernization of air operations and the adoption of next-generation aircraft. The Company currently operates one of the largest commuter airlines in the United States by scheduled departures and provides private charter services. Together, these businesses provide the operational scale and real-world operating data to validate and deploy its software. These capabilities position Surf Air Mobility as a leader shaping a more efficient, connected, and accessible future for aviation. Such risks and uncertainties include, among many others: Surf Air Mobility’s ability to anticipate the future needs of the air mobility market; Surf Air Mobility’s future ability to pay contractual obligations and liquidity, which will depend on operating performance, cash flow and ability to secure adequate financing; the dependence on third-party partners and suppliers for the components and collaboration in Surf Air Mobility’s development of its advanced air mobility software platform, and any interruptions, disagreements or delays with those partners and suppliers; the inability to execute business objectives and growth strategies successfully or sustain Surf Air Mobility’s growth; the inability of Surf Air Mobility’s customers to pay for Surf Air Mobility’s services; the inability of Surf Air Mobility to obtain additional financing or access the capital markets to fund its ongoing operations on acceptable terms and conditions; the outcome of any legal proceedings that might be instituted against Surf Air Mobility, the risks associated with Surf Air Mobility’s obligations to comply with applicable laws, government regulations and rules and standards of the New York Stock Exchange; and general economic conditions. title: Employee Background Verification in India: Process, Cost & Compliance Checklist
summary: Learn employee background verification in India, including BGV process, legal compliance, costs, and best practices.
body_text: Insights & Resources Employee Background Verification in India: Process, Cost & Compliance Checklist July 14, 2026 Shashank Yadav No comments yet Introduction Hiring the right talent is the cornerstone of building a successful business. Yet, in an increasingly competitive job market, not every candidate presents an entirely truthful picture of their qualifications and experience. Employee background verification (BGV) has emerged as an indispensable step in the hiring process for Indian employers, protecting organisations from fraud, legal liability, and reputational damage. According to SHRM India, approximately 5 to 12 percent of Indian candidates misrepresent at least one element of their profile, ranging from inflated educational credentials to fabricated employment histories. For small and medium businesses, a single bad hire can cascade into financial losses, legal complications, and team morale issues. This comprehensive guide walks you through every aspect of employee background verification in India — the process, types, costs, legal compliance, and actionable checklists to help you hire with confidence in 2026. What Is Employee Background Verification? Employee background verification is a systematic process of validating the information provided by a job candidate — including their identity, educational qualifications, employment history, criminal record, and financial standing. The primary purpose is to ensure that the person you are hiring is who they claim to be, possesses the credentials they have listed, and does not pose a risk to your organisation. BGV can be broadly divided into two categories: Pre-employment verification: Conducted before a candidate officially joins the organisation. This is the most common form and typically covers identity, education, previous employment, and criminal checks. It serves as a gatekeeping mechanism to filter out candidates who misrepresent their backgrounds. Post-employment verification: Performed after the employee has joined, often triggered by a promotion, role change, or periodic compliance audit. Industries such as banking, financial services, and IT frequently mandate ongoing verification to maintain regulatory compliance. Both types serve the same fundamental objective: reducing organisational risk. Whether you are a startup hiring your tenth employee or an enterprise onboarding hundreds of new recruits each quarter, background verification provides an essential layer of due diligence that protects your people, your clients, and your reputation. Why Background Verification Is Critical for Indian Businesses The cost of a bad hire extends far beyond the salary paid. Industry estimates suggest that a single bad hire can cost an Indian company anywhere from Rs 5 lakh to Rs 50 lakh when factoring in recruitment expenses, training costs, lost productivity, potential legal fees, and the time spent managing the fallout. For small businesses operating on thin margins, this figure can be existential. Key Reasons BGV Matters Financial protection: Fraudulent employees can engage in embezzlement, intellectual property theft, or vendor kickback schemes. A thorough background check significantly reduces these risks by identifying candidates with questionable histories. Legal liability: Employers can face negligent hiring lawsuits if an employee causes harm and the organisation failed to conduct reasonable pre-employment screening. Indian courts have increasingly held employers accountable for due diligence failures. Workplace safety: Verifying criminal records and past conduct helps create a safer work environment. This is particularly crucial for roles that involve access to vulnerable populations, confidential data, or physical assets. Regulatory compliance: Specific industries carry mandatory verification requirements. The IT/ITES sector follows NASSCOM-DSCI guidelines. The BFSI sector must comply with RBI and SEBI directives on employee screening. Healthcare employers must verify medical certifications and licensing. Client and partner confidence: Many enterprise clients, particularly multinational corporations, require their vendors and partners to demonstrate robust employee screening processes. Background verification is often a prerequisite for winning large contracts. In summary, background verification is not just a human resources formality — it is a strategic risk management tool that protects your bottom line, your workforce, and your business relationships. Types of Background Checks in India India offers a diverse range of background verification services, each addressing a specific dimension of candidate due diligence. Understanding these types helps employers design a verification package tailored to their industry, role requirements, and budget. 1. Identity Verification (Aadhaar, PAN, Passport) The foundational layer of any background check. Identity verification confirms the candidate’s legal identity using government-issued documents such as Aadhaar, PAN card, passport, or voter ID. Modern digital verification platforms can validate these documents in real time via DigiLocker and UIDAI APIs. Typical turnaround is same-day, with costs ranging from Rs 50 to Rs 150 per check. 2. Education Verification Education verification confirms the candidate’s academic credentials by cross-referencing claims with the issuing institution or the National Academic Depository (NAD). This includes degree certificates, mark sheets, and professional certifications. Education fraud remains one of the most common forms of misrepresentation in India. Turnaround time is typically 5 to 10 working days, with costs between Rs 200 and Rs 500 per verification. 3. Employment History Verification This check validates the candidate’s previous employers, designations held, tenure, and reasons for leaving. Verification is conducted by contacting the HR departments of former employers directly. Discrepancies in employment history — such as inflated job titles or concealed terminations, are surprisingly common. Each employer verification takes 5 to 7 working days and costs Rs 300 to Rs 600. 4. Criminal Record Check Criminal background checks involve searching district and high court records, police station databases, and national crime databases. In India, court records are not fully digitised, making this process more time-intensive than in countries with centralised databases. Some employers also request police verification, which involves physical verification at the candidate’s local police station. Turnaround is 7 to 14 working days, with costs between Rs 500 and Rs 1,500. 5. Address Verification Address verification confirms the candidate’s current and permanent residential addresses. This can be done through physical field visits, postal verification, or digital means using Aadhaar-based address validation. Physical verification provides the highest confidence level but is more expensive and time-consuming. Turnaround is 3 to 7 working days, costing Rs 250 to Rs 500. 6. Reference Checks Professional reference checks involve contacting individuals provided by the candidate — typically former managers or colleagues — to validate claims about work performance, conduct, and character. Well-conducted reference checks can reveal insights that no document can capture, such as interpersonal skills, work ethic, and cultural fit. These take 3 to 5 working days and cost Rs 300 to Rs 600. 7. Credit History Check (CIBIL) For roles in the BFSI sector or positions involving financial responsibility, a credit history check via CIBIL, Experian, or Equifax reveals the candidate’s financial behaviour, including outstanding debts, defaults, and credit score. This check is particularly relevant for roles such as accountants, treasury managers, and financial advisors. Turnaround is 1 to 2 working days, costing Rs 200 to Rs 400. 8. Drug Screening While not yet widespread in India, drug screening is increasingly adopted for safety-critical roles in manufacturing, transportation, mining, and healthcare. Pre-employment drug tests typically screen for common substances and are conducted at certified laboratories. Employers must establish a clear substance abuse policy before implementing drug testing to ensure legal compliance. Check Type Turnaround Cost (Rs) Priority Best For Identity Verification Same-day 50-150 Essential All roles Education Verification 5-10 days 200-500 Essential All roles Employment History 5-7 days/employer 300-600 Essential All roles Criminal Record 7-14 days 500-1,500 High All roles Address Verification 3-7 days 250-500 High Field/remote roles Reference Checks 3-5 days 300-600 Medium Mid-senior roles Credit History (CIBIL) 1-2 days 200-400 Industry-specific BFSI, finance Drug Screening 2-5 days 500-2,000 Role-specific Safety-critical Step-by-Step Background Verification Process A well-structured background verification process ensures thoroughness, compliance, and efficiency. Here is the recommended ten-step approach for Indian employers: Obtain Written Consent from the Candidate — Under the DPDP Act 2023, you must secure explicit, informed consent from the candidate before initiating any background check. Use a clearly worded consent form that specifies the types of checks being conducted, the data being collected, and the purpose of the verification. Collect Documents and References — Request copies of identity documents (Aadhaar, PAN, passport), educational certificates, previous employment offer and relieving letters, salary slips, and contact details for professional references. Initiate Checks via Internal Team or Vendor — Decide whether to handle verification in-house or through a specialised BGV vendor. For companies processing fewer than 20 hires per month, outsourcing is typically more cost-effective and reliable. Verify Identity — Run Aadhaar and PAN verification through authorised digital platforms. Cross-reference the candidate’s photo, name, and date of birth across submitted documents to detect inconsistencies. Education and Employment Verification — Contact universities, colleges, and former employers to validate the candidate’s academic qualifications and work history. Use the National Academic Depository for faster education verification where available. Criminal and Court Record Checks — Search district court databases, high court records, and national crime registries. For senior roles, consider extending this to multiple jurisdictions where the candidate has previously resided. Address Verification — Confirm residential addresses through physical field visits or digital validation. Physical verification is recommended for roles that involve handling cash, valuables, or access to client premises. Compile Report and Adjudication — Aggregate all verification findings into a structured report. Classify each check as Verified, Minor Discrepancy, or Major Discrepancy. Establish clear adjudication criteria for how discrepancies will be evaluated. Make the Hiring Decision — Review the verification report with the hiring manager. Minor discrepancies, such as a slight variation in employment dates, may be acceptable. Major discrepancies, such as a fake degree or concealed criminal record, should result in offer withdrawal. Securely Store Verification Records — Retain all verification documents in a secure, access-controlled digital repository. Under the DPDP Act, you must define clear retention periods and ensure that data is deleted when no longer needed for the stated purpose. Cost of Background Verification in India The cost of background verification in India varies significantly depending on the depth and breadth of checks required. Most BGV vendors offer tiered packages to accommodate different budgets and needs: Package Cost (Rs) Includes Basic 800-2,000 Identity verification (Aadhaar/PAN) + Education verification + Address verification Standard 2,000-4,000 Basic package + Employment history (1-2 employers) + Criminal record check + Reference check (1 reference) Comprehensive 4,000-8,000+ Standard package + Employment history (all employers) + Court record checks (multiple jurisdictions) + Credit check + Drug screening + Global database search Factors Affecting BGV Cost Number of checks: Each additional verification type adds to the total cost. Employers should prioritise checks based on role sensitivity rather than running every available check for every hire. Geographical coverage: Multi-city or multi-state checks cost more due to the need for local court searches and physical verifications across jurisdictions. Turnaround time: Expedited checks attract a premium of 20 to 50 percent over standard timelines. Candidate’s background complexity: Candidates with extensive work history, international education, or multiple addresses require more verification effort. Volume discounts: Most vendors offer discounts of 15 to 20 percent for companies processing more than 50 verifications per month. Large enterprises processing 500 or more verifications monthly can negotiate discounts of up to 30 percent. For most Indian SMEs, the Standard package at Rs 2,000 to Rs 4,000 per candidate provides the optimal balance of thoroughness and cost-effectiveness. Reserve comprehensive packages for senior leadership roles, positions with financial authority, or roles in regulated industries. Legal and Compliance Framework India does not have a single, unified law mandating background verification for private-sector employers. Instead, the legal landscape is shaped by a combination of data protection legislation, industry-specific regulations, and state-level employment laws. Understanding this framework is essential for conducting legally defensible background checks. The Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act 2023 The DPDP Act 2023 is the most significant recent legislation affecting background verification practices in India. Key provisions include: Written consent: Employers must obtain explicit, informed consent from candidates before collecting or processing any personal data for verification purposes. Consent must be specific, freely given, and easy to withdraw. Purpose limitation: Personal data collected during the BGV process can only be used for the stated purpose of employment verification. Repurposing this data for marketing, profiling, or other unrelated activities is prohibited. Data minimisation: Collect only the data that is strictly necessary for the verification. Avoid gathering information that is not directly relevant to the candidate’s suitability for the role. Storage limitation: Define and enforce clear data retention periods. Verification records should not be retained indefinitely. Establish policies for secure deletion once the retention period expires. Penalties: Non-compliance can attract penalties of up to Rs 250 crore , making adherence non-negotiable for employers of all sizes. Industry-Specific Regulations RBI Guidelines (BFSI): The Reserve Bank of India mandates thorough background screening for employees in banking and financial services, including credit checks and criminal record verification. Non-compliance can result in regulatory sanctions. SEBI Requirements: Securities and Exchange Board of India requires background verification for key managerial personnel in capital market intermediaries, mutual fund houses, and listed companies. NASSCOM/DSCI Guidelines (IT/ITES): The National Association of Software and Service Companies, in collaboration with the Data Security Council of India, has established comprehensive BGV guidelines for the IT/ITES sector. These guidelines recommend a standardised verification framework and are widely adopted across the industry. State Shops & Establishments Acts: Various states have employment regulations under their respective Shops and Establishments Acts that may include provisions related to employee verification, record-keeping, and compliance. Employers must ensure they comply with the regulations applicable in their state of operation. DPDP Act 2023 Compliance Checklist for BGV Use this checklist to ensure your background verification process complies with the Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023: # Requirement Action Required 1 Written Consent Draft a clear, jargon-free consent form specifying each type of check, data collected, and processing purpose. Obtain signed consent before initiating any verification. 2 Purpose Specification Document the specific purpose for each type of data collected. Ensure data is used only for employment verification and not repurposed. 3 Data Minimisation Audit your data collection forms to remove fields that are not strictly necessary. Collect only data relevant to the role and checks being performed. 4 Storage Limitation Define retention periods for each data category (e.g., 3 years for verified employees, 6 months for rejected candidates). Implement automated deletion workflows. 5 Vendor Agreements Execute data processing agreements with all BGV vendors specifying data handling obligations, security requirements, sub-processing restrictions, and breach notification timelines. 6 Breach Notification Establish an incident response plan for data breaches involving BGV data. Ensure you can notify the Data Protection Board and affected individuals within mandated timelines. 7 Candidate Rights Create processes for candidates to access, correct, or request deletion of their verification data. Ensure withdrawal of consent is straightforward and honoured promptly. 8 Cross-Border Transfers If using international BGV vendors, ensure data transfers comply with DPDP cross-border transfer provisions. Maintain records of all cross-border data flows. How to Choose a Background Verification Vendor Selecting the right BGV vendor is critical to the success of your verification programme. The wrong vendor can lead to inaccurate results, compliance violations, and hiring delays. Evaluate potential vendors against these criteria: Turnaround time: The vendor should offer clearly defined timelines for each check type and consistently meet them. Delays in verification can cause candidates to accept competing offers. Accuracy and depth: Prioritise vendors with proven accuracy rates above 99 percent. Ask for case studies and client references. Verify that they use primary sources rather than relying solely on database searches. DPDP Act compliance: Ensure the vendor has robust data protection practices, including encrypted data storage, access controls, secure transmission protocols, and documented data retention and deletion policies. Technology platform: Modern vendors offer API-based integrations, real-time dashboards, automated status updates, and candidate-facing portals. These features significantly reduce administrative overhead. Pricing transparency: Avoid vendors with hidden fees. Request a detailed cost breakdown for each check type and understand what is included in bundled packages versus what incurs additional charges. Geographic coverage: If you hire across multiple Indian states or internationally, ensure the vendor has physical verification capability and court access in all required jurisdictions. Industry specialisation: Some vendors specialise in specific sectors such as BFSI, IT, healthcare, or manufacturing. Sector-specific expertise translates to faster processing and more relevant checks. Common Red Flags in Background Checks Background verification is only valuable if your team knows how to interpret the results. Watch for these common red flags: Degree discrepancies: The candidate claims a degree from a university that has no record of their enrolment, or the degree title, year of passing, or grade does not match the institution’s records. Fake degree mills remain a significant problem in India. Fabricated experience letters: The company listed as a previous employer has no record of the candidate, or the HR department confirms different dates, designation, or reason for leaving than what the candidate provided. Unexplained employment gaps: While career gaps are not inherently negative, gaps that the candidate did not disclose or cannot explain may warrant further investigation. Criminal records: Any undisclosed criminal history, pending court cases, or ongoing investigations should be treated as a serious red flag, particularly for roles involving financial responsibility or access to sensitive information. Address mismatches: The candidate’s stated address does not match physical verification findings, or the address provided does not exist. This may indicate an attempt to conceal true residential history. Inconsistent reference feedback: References provide accounts that significantly contradict the candidate’s claims about their role, responsibilities, or performance at previous organisations. Industry-Specific BGV Requirements Different industries face distinct risk profiles and regulatory obligations that shape their background verification requirements: IT/ITES The IT sector typically requires identity verification, education verification, employment history, criminal checks, and address verification for all hires. Companies handling international client data often add global database searches and credit checks for senior roles. NASSCOM-DSCI guidelines serve as the industry standard. BFSI (Banking, Financial Services & Insurance) The most heavily regulated sector for employee screening. RBI mandates criminal record checks, credit history verification, and education validation for all employees. Senior roles require enhanced due diligence, including directorship searches and regulatory action checks. SEBI adds requirements for key managerial personnel in capital market entities. Healthcare Healthcare employers must verify medical licenses, certifications, and registration with state medical councils. Criminal background checks are critical given patient safety implications. Drug screening is recommended for clinical staff. Manufacturing Manufacturing companies prioritise identity verification, criminal checks, and address verification. Drug screening is important for roles operating heavy machinery. Safety certifications and previous incident records should be verified for supervisory roles. Government Contractors Companies working on government contracts often face enhanced security clearance requirements. These may include comprehensive criminal checks across all jurisdictions, financial integrity verification, and character investigation through multiple reference checks and neighbourhood verification. How SalaryBox Helps with Employee Verification Managing the employee verification process alongside hiring, onboarding, and compliance can overwhelm lean HR teams. SalaryBox simplifies and streamlines this entire workflow through its integrated employee management platform. Digital Onboarding: SalaryBox’s digital onboarding workflow allows you to collect candidate documents, identity proofs, and consent forms electronically — eliminating paper-based processes and ensuring nothing falls through the cracks. Document Management: Store and organise all employee documents securely in one place. From Aadhaar copies and educational certificates to verification reports and consent forms, everything is accessible, searchable, and audit-ready. Compliance Tracking: SalaryBox helps you track verification statuses, document expiry dates, and compliance deadlines. Automated reminders ensure that renewals and re-verifications are completed on time. Team Visibility: Give hiring managers and compliance officers real-time visibility into the verification status of each candidate, enabling faster and more informed hiring decisions. Start streamlining your employee verification and onboarding process today. Frequently Asked Questions 1. Is background verification mandatory for private employers in India? There is no single central law that mandates background verification for all private employers in India. However, specific industries such as BFSI (regulated by RBI and SEBI) and IT/ITES (guided by NASSCOM-DSCI frameworks) have sector-specific requirements. Additionally, the DPDP Act 2023 imposes strict obligations on how personal data is collected and processed during BGV, making compliance essential even where verification itself is not mandated. 2. How long does the entire background verification process take? The timeline depends on the types of checks being conducted. A basic package covering identity and education verification can be completed in 3 to 5 working days. A comprehensive package including criminal checks, employment history, and address verification typically takes 10 to 21 working days. Delays are most common in criminal record checks due to the partially manual nature of court record searches in India. 3. Can a candidate refuse to undergo background verification? Yes, a candidate has the right to refuse background verification. Under the DPDP Act 2023, consent must be freely given and cannot be coerced. However, employers are equally within their rights to make a successful background check a condition of employment. If a candidate refuses, the employer may choose to withdraw the offer, provided this condition was communicated upfront in the offer letter or employment terms. 4. What happens if a discrepancy is found during verification? The course of action depends on the severity and nature of the discrepancy. Minor discrepancies — such as a slight difference in employment dates or a variation in the designation title — may be resolved by seeking clarification from the candidate. Major discrepancies — such as a fake degree, fabricated employment history, or undisclosed criminal record — typically result in offer withdrawal or termination if the employee has already joined. Employers should document their adjudication criteria and apply them consistently to avoid claims of discriminatory treatment. 5. Is background verification conducted before or after joining? Best practice is to conduct background verification before the candidate joins (pre-employment verification). However, in time-sensitive hiring scenarios, some employers allow candidates to join provisionally while verification is in progress. In such cases, the offer letter should clearly state that employment is contingent on successful completion of BGV, and the employer reserves the right to terminate if adverse findings surface. 6. How should employers handle BGV data after the hiring decision is made? Under the DPDP Act 2023, employers must define clear data retention periods for BGV records. For candidates who are hired, verification records are typically retained for the duration of employment plus a defined post-employment period (commonly 1 to 3 years). For candidates who are rejected, verification data should be securely deleted within 6 months of the hiring decision unless a longer period is justified by a specific legal obligation. All data must be stored with appropriate security measures and access controls. Related Shashank Yadav Leave a Reply Cancel reply

title: 1968–70 Plymouth Road Runners Aren’t Walking Away with Younger Buyers Just Yet
summary: In the horsepower heyday of the late ’60s, there was a muscle car for every buyer. The archetypal Pontiac GTO could be had in several iterations from sinister to ostentatious. Chevrolet’s Chevelle came with brawny big-block power in an understated wrapping. Buick and Olds had GS and 4-4-2 offerings with their own flavor of V-8s. […]
body_text: In the horsepower heyday of the late ’60s, there was a muscle car for every buyer. The archetypal Pontiac GTO could be had in several iterations from sinister to ostentatious. Chevrolet’s Chevelle came with brawny big-block power in an understated wrapping. Buick and Olds had GS and 4-4-2 offerings with their own flavor of V-8s. Charger offered unique, Coke-bottle bodywork to go with its all-big-block engine lineup. Rambler’s conservative lines could be transformed by patriotic red, white, and blue livery in the SC/Rambler. Ford’s sinewy Torino came with contrasting graphics and blacked-out hoods complete with gaping scoops. At Plymouth, meanwhile, buyers could opt for a more serious and luxurious GTX or the cheerful and chirpy Road Runner ( Acceleratti Incredibilus) . Plymouth Plymouth split its completely redesigned 1968 B-body (shared with the Dodge Coroner and Charger) lineup into five columns: GTX, Sport Satellite, Satellite, Road Runner, and Belvedere. While the GTX and Road Runner shared sheet metal—including the side-scoop hood—the Road Runner offered a lower cost of entry with a hardtop-style roof that gave the front door frameless glass but included a B-pillar and tilt-out quarter glass. A hardtop, identical to the GTX with roll-down quarter glass, was a later addition to the lineup. Both of the sporty Plymouth B-body muscle cars could be optioned with the mammoth 426 Hemi with twin four-barrel carburetors. GTX came standard with a 375hp 440. The playful, more affordable Road Runner, marketed as “Private property of the young and aware,” came standard with a 335hp 383 big-block that it didn’t share with any other Mopar muscle car. Its 5-hp bump over the Super Commando 383 found in other Mopars was thanks to the camshaft from the high-performance 440. Speaking of the 440, it wasn’t initially available in the Road Runner. Brandan Gillogly Of course, several key components came with the Road Runner that just weren’t found in any other Mopar muscle car. Its horn, labeled with a decal noting “Voice of Road Runner,” was emblazoned with the Warner Brothers cartoon of the same name and its signature goofy grin. It gave the car its signature sound and was eventually finished in purple to match the cartoon bird’s wings and crest. There were also cartoon Road Runners on the doors, decklid, and instrument panel. Eventually, the speedy Southwesterner’s nemesis, Wile E. Coyote ( Carnivorous Vulgaris ), could also be found on one of our favorite air cleaner decals of all time. The 1968 Road Runner used a flat black horn. The later models embraced the cartoon bird’s color palette and went with purple. Brandan Gillogly 1969 1969 brought the Road Runner an updated look with freshened sheet metal. Up front, the basic quad-headlight design remained, but with new bezels and a similar grille shape, now divided into fewer rectangles. Along with the rest of its Mopar siblings, Road Runner got rectangular side marker lights, replacing the small, circular lights that Mopars wore in 1968. At the back of the car, square, concave taillights nestled into the quarter panels. It was also the first time that Road Runner was offered as a convertible. Partway through the model year, a new engine option was added: the 390hp, 3×2 version of the 440. Brandan Gillogly 1970 More significant design changes came in 1970, with another set of new fenders and a racetrack grille up front that previewed the chrome bumper coming for the fuselage-body redesign of 1971 B-bodies. A new bumper carried round marker lights. The quarter panels got non-functional scoops, and the rear fascia got a completely new look with horizontal stripes for taillights. Brandan Gillogly The Road Runner soldiered on in various forms until 1980, when it was a package on the compact F-body Volaré platform. Today, the first generation 1968–70 Road Runners are established classic Mopar muscle cars with a solid fan base and support. The most affordable iteration of the 1968–70 Plymouth Road Runner is the 383-powered 1968 coupe with a #2 (excellent) value of $55,300. The hardtop carries an 8.5% premium. Naturally, convertibles also demand a premium. No matter the body style, any 1968–70 Road Runner is worth at least double when equipped with a 426 Hemi when compared to the base 383 V-8. With fewer than 11,000 produced for general consumption and far fewer than that left, the street Hemi remains a big draw. Other value differentiators include transmissions (four-speeds can command a 10% premium) and paint. In the vintage Mopar world, colors can make an astonishing difference in both value and salability. Brandan Gillogly Hagerty Senior Auction Editor Andrew Newton took a look at the current state of the Plymouth Roadrunner market and pulled out some interesting numbers. “These were hit hard by the late 2000s muscle car bust,” says Newton. “From January 2007 to January 2010, average #2 value dropped 29%. Prices have rebounded quite a bit, as Road Runner’s average #2 value is up 27% over the last 10 years, including an 18% increase in just the last five years. Unfortunately, Newton also noted that inflation over the last five years is more than 20%, keeping those values gains in check. Certain variations of Road Runner also haven’t even recovered from their pre-recession highs, without accounting for inflation. Looking at the collector market as a whole, baby boomers make up 34%, Gen X 31%, millennials 20%, and Gen Z 10%. We’re not surprised to find that insurance quotes for ’60s and ‘70s muscle cars favor older buyers, but a lot more younger buyers are picking up contemporary Chargers and Chevelles. Gen X interest in 1968–70 Chargers is 30% higher than Road Runner, and millennial interest in 1968–72 Chevelle is 50% higher. You can credit at least a bit of that to the pop culture staying power of both of those models for keeping them relevant, and pushing demand a bit higher. Meanwhile, Plymouth is a defunct brand and has been for 25 years, and the Road Runner’s fairly high price also puts it out of reach for many young enthusiasts. We haven’t missed the irony that it’s the older buyers who remain more interested in a car marketed by a Saturday morning cartoon character. Still, it’s hard to bet against the 1968–70 Road Runner. There are enough subtle variations in each production year for a collector to find a favorite look, and the hourglass body lines built into each one give it classic Mopar muscle style. Standard big-block V-8 power under the hood is, naturally, another big draw. As with other niches in the collector market, like sports cars or vintage 4x4s, a slightly less popular model like the Road Runner could lag behind many of the more popular models in its category until enough buyers realize what they’ve been overlooking. The post 1968–70 Plymouth Road Runners Aren’t Walking Away with Younger Buyers Just Yet appeared first on Hagerty Media .

summary: Affordable and scalable effector will strengthen RAF stockpile resilienceLONDON, July 21, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Farnborough International Airshow – Raytheon UK, part of RTX's (NYSE: RTX) Raytheon business, today introduced Red Kite®, its first sovereign precision weapon fully designed and digitally engineered in the United Kingdom.Developed with a consortium of British defence partners, Red Kite is an affordable, highly deployable precision weapon that advances the UK's ability to rapidly scale critical stockpiles. Using advanced digital modelling technologies, the effector quickly moved from concept to prototype.
body_text: Raytheon UK unveils sovereign, digitally engineered precision weapon Red Kite July 21, 2026 Share this article on Facebook Share this article on Twitter Share this article on LinkedIn Share this article via email Affordable and scalable effector will strengthen RAF stockpile resilience LONDON , July 21, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Farnborough International Airshow – Raytheon UK, part of RTX's (NYSE: RTX) Raytheon business, today introduced Red Kite®, its first sovereign precision weapon fully designed and digitally engineered in the United Kingdom. Developed with a consortium of British defence partners, Red Kite is an affordable, highly deployable precision weapon that advances the UK's ability to rapidly scale critical stockpiles. Using advanced digital modelling technologies, the effector quickly moved from concept to prototype. "Red Kite was designed with affordability and adaptability in mind, and marks a significant step forward for UK defence," said James Gray, managing director and chief executive of Raytheon UK. "Working closely with our partners over the past five years, we've combined innovative design, digital engineering and proven technologies to develop a sovereign capability for the RAF faster and more efficiently than ever." Red Kite uses the existing Stormbreaker® airframe and can be integrated across a wide range of air platforms. It builds on Raytheon UK's extensive experience delivering precision weapons, including Paveway IV and adds a cost-effective, high-volume capability that enhances RAF operational flexibility. "Red Kite is about getting capability to the frontline faster – reducing cost, increasing availability and meeting our customers' needs when it matters most," added Gray. "It represents a clear step toward a more resilient, sovereign UK defence industrial base." Red Kite will be delivered through a nationwide UK supply chain, bringing together specialist design, engineering and manufacturing expertise from across the country. From systems electronics and software in Harlow to control actuation systems in Glenrothes, the programme will sustain high-skilled jobs, advanced manufacturing and sovereign defence capabilities across England, Scotland and Wales. Raytheon UK estimates that approximately 140 highly skilled jobs will directly support this program. About Raytheon UK With over 2,000 employees in the UK, Raytheon UK is a major supplier and systems integrator to the UK Ministry of Defence that designs, develops and manufactures defence and space products. The company is also a leading provider of training transformations services and continues to invest in research and development, supporting innovation and technological advances across the country. Raytheon UK is part of RTX's Raytheon business. About Raytheon Raytheon, an RTX business, is a leading provider of defense solutions to help the U.S. government, our allies and partners defend their national sovereignty and ensure their security. For more than 100 years, Raytheon has developed new technologies and enhanced existing capabilities in integrated air and missile defense, smart weapons, missiles, advanced sensors and radars, interceptors, space-based systems, hypersonics and missile defense across land, air, sea and space. About RTX With more than 180,000 global employees, we push the limits of technology and science to redefine how we connect and protect our world. With industry-leading capabilities, we advance aviation, engineer integrated defense systems for operational success, and develop next-generation technology solutions and manufacturing to help global customers address their most critical challenges. The company, with 2025 sales of more than $88 billion, is headquartered in Arlington, Virginia. For questions or to schedule an interview, please contact [email protected] . title: Tactile Medical Enters Exclusive U.S. Distribution Agreement with ElastiMed for its MyoSleeve™ Wearable Compression Device for VA and DoD Patients
summary: The Investor Relations website contains information about Tactile Systems Technology, Inc. 's business for stockholders, potential investors, and financial analysts.
body_text: Discreet, Battery-Powered Device Reaches Patients at Earlier Stages of Disease Progression MINNEAPOLIS, July 13, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Tactile Systems Technology, Inc. (“Tactile Medical”; the “Company”) (Nasdaq: TCMD), a medical technology company providing therapies for people with chronic disorders, today announced it has entered into an exclusive distribution agreement with ElastiMed, Inc. to bring MyoSleeve™, its discreet, wearable non-pneumatic compression device for the lower leg, to Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) and Department of Defense (DoD) patients across the United States. MyoSleeve expands Tactile Medical’s established market-leading portfolio by providing a new treatment option for appropriately selected patients in earlier stages of chronic swelling who may not yet require more intensive compression therapy. MyoSleeve may also be appropriate as a complementary treatment to a traditional pneumatic compression device and for patients who struggle with conservative therapy, or those with mobility-limiting cases. Wrapped around the calf with the ability to be worn beneath clothing, MyoSleeve uses electroactive polymer technology to deliver dynamic compression through flexible bands that contract in sequence. The battery-powered device is designed as an all-in-one therapy option, operating without tubing, cords, or an external controller, and quietly delivers intermittent therapy while patients go about daily activities. MyoSleeve has received U.S. Food and Drug Administration 510(k) clearance and is indicated for the treatment of chronic swelling, including chronic edema, lymphedema, and venous insufficiency. Under the agreement, Tactile Medical holds exclusive U.S. distribution rights for MyoSleeve within the VA and DoD systems. In connection with these exclusive distribution rights, the Company made an upfront payment of $3 million to ElastiMed. The Company also committed to certain minimum purchase obligations and marketing and sales promotion as it supports ElastiMed’s growth. The Company expects to leverage its established sales organization, billing and payment expertise, and patient support infrastructure to drive MyoSleeve commercialization and support ongoing market access initiatives. MyoSleeve is available by prescription, and appropriate patient selection is determined by the treating clinician. “Our agreement with ElastiMed adds a differentiated, wearable compression option to Tactile Medical’s portfolio and reflects our strategy of expanding access to patient-focused solutions across the continuum of chronic swelling care,” said Sheri Dodd, Chief Executive Officer of Tactile Medical. “For the right patient, MyoSleeve offers unobtrusive compression therapy that fits into daily life, giving patients the freedom to stay mobile while engaged in their own care.” “Partnering with Tactile Medical gives MyoSleeve a direct path to certain patients with chronic swelling who want to stay active while getting the treatment they need,” said Omer Zelka, Chief Executive Officer of ElastiMed. “It is the first ambulatory all-in-one, cable-free, clinical-grade solution for patients with venous and lymphatic conditions. This partnership enables the first commercial introduction of MyoSleeve through a trusted and market-leading medical device partner.” “Compression therapy is not one-size-fits-all. Clinicians achieve the best outcomes when they have a range of options that can be matched to disease severity, anatomy, and lifestyle,” said Tony Gasparis, MD, Chief Medical Officer of Tactile Medical. “MyoSleeve introduces an important new option for appropriately selected patients with lower-leg swelling, offering active compression that is well-suited for earlier stages of disease, where consistent therapy adherence is key to slowing disease progression. Importantly, MyoSleeve is designed to complement — not replace — advanced pneumatic compression therapies, which remain the standard of care for patients with more extensive or advanced disease.” For more information about MyoSleeve, please visit https://tactilemedical.com/myosleeve/ . About Tactile Systems Technology, Inc. (DBA Tactile Medical) Tactile Medical is a leader in developing and marketing at-home therapies for people suffering from underserved, chronic conditions including lymphedema, lipedema, chronic venous insufficiency and chronic inflammatory lung disease by helping them live better and care for themselves. Tactile Medical collaborates with clinicians to expand clinical evidence, raise awareness, increase access to care, reduce overall healthcare costs and improve the quality of life for tens of thousands of patients each year. About ElastiMed, Inc. ElastiMed is a commercial-stage medical device company developing wearable therapeutic devices based on electroactive polymer (EAP) technology, designed to deliver dynamic compression in a comfortable, low-profile, and easy-to-use form. Investor Inquiries: Sam Bentzinger Gilmartin Group [email protected]

title: Kalaris Appoints Laurie Keating to Board of Directors
summary: Highly experienced biotechnology executive and board member will assist Kalaris in achieving its next phase of growth...
body_text: BERKELEY HEIGHTS, N.J., July 06, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Kalaris Therapeutics, Inc. (Nasdaq: KLRS) (“Kalaris”), a clinical-stage biopharmaceutical company dedicated to the development and commercialization of treatments for prevalent retinal diseases, today announced the appointment of Laurie Keating to its Board of Directors, effective August 1, 2026. In conjunction with the announcement of Ms. Keating’s appointment, Morana Jovan-Embiricos is stepping down from the Board of Directors. “We’re delighted to welcome Laurie to the Kalaris Board of Directors. She has extensive strategic, operational, and legal expertise spanning multiple therapeutic areas and development stages. Laurie will be an outstanding addition to our Board, and we look forward to her contributions and guidance as we continue to grow Kalaris,” said David Hallal, Chairman of the Kalaris Board of Directors. “I also want to thank Morana for her service to Kalaris over the past year. She was a valuable member of our Board and helped us make significant advances in the development of TH103 and in our evolution as a public biotech company.” Laurie Keating said, “I am thrilled to be joining Kalaris’ Board of Directors. I look forward to contributing to the company’s continued success and collaborating with the leadership team as they seek to transform the lives of patients with retinal diseases.” Laurie currently serves as Chair of the Board of Directors of PepGen (Nasdaq: PEPG) and as a member of the Board of Directors of Immuneering Corp (Nasdaq: IMRX). She formerly served on the Board of Directors of Imago Biosciences (acquired by Merck), Imbria Pharmaceuticals, and the Massachusetts Biotechnology Council (MassBio). Laurie previously served as the Executive Vice President, General Counsel and Corporate Secretary of Alnylam Pharmaceuticals. In this role she oversaw global government affairs, legal, IP, litigation, and compliance teams and advised the Board of Directors on financing and strategic collaborations, governance, and corporate strategy. Prior to Alnylam, she served as SVP, General Counsel and Corporate Secretary of Millennium Pharmaceuticals, a commercial stage biopharmaceutical company that was acquired by Takeda Pharmaceuticals. Laurie earned her Bachelor’s degree in economics from the University of California at Berkeley, and her JD from the University of California, Hastings College of the Law. About TH103 TH103 is an investigational dual-targeting biologic engineered by VEGF scientific discoverer Dr. Napoleone Ferrara to achieve extended intraocular retention with enhanced VEGF inhibition through optimized binding to VEGF receptor 1 ligands and concurrent heparan sulfate proteoglycan (HSPG) anchoring. It is a fully humanized, recombinant fusion protein designed for intravitreal delivery, with potential applications as a treatment for exudative and/or neovascular retinal diseases, such as wet AMD, diabetic eye disease and retinal vein occlusion. TH103 is currently being investigated in a Phase 1b/2 clinical trial in patients with neovascular Age-related Macular Degeneration (nAMD). About Kalaris Kalaris Therapeutics is a clinical-stage biopharmaceutical company dedicated to the development and commercialization of treatments for prevalent retinal diseases. Founded by renowned scientist Dr. Napoleone Ferrara, whose pioneering research led to the development of anti-VEGF therapy, the company is committed to advancing novel therapeutic approaches for patients with sight-threatening retinal conditions with major unmet medical needs. For more information, visit www.kalaristx.com . Kalaris Therapeutics Investor Contact: Corey Davis, Ph.D. LifeSci Advisors, LLC +1 212 915 2577 cdavis@lifesciadvisors.com ir@kalaristx.com

title: The new rules of collaboration for IT leaders
summary: Your collaboration environment probably wasn't designed. It evolved. Here's what that means for IT teams managing the growing gap between how employees work and how collaboration is governed.
body_text: Most enterprise collaboration environments didn't start with a blueprint. They started with a few urgent procurement decisions, a decade of incremental additions, and a lot of "good enough for now." Nobody designed the current state. It accumulated. That was manageable when collaboration meant meetings plus email. But meetings, chat, phone, docs, AI, and workflows now operate as a single connected layer. Employees already treat them that way. They move from a meeting summary to a chat thread to a shared document to a task list without thinking about which tool they're in. IT governance, for the most part, hasn't caught up with that reality. The gap between how work actually happens and how IT manages the tools behind it can create fragmentation, inconsistent security posture, and blind spots that compound quietly over time. This piece maps what changed, why it matters, and what a collaboration environment built for this reality actually requires. How collaboration stacks got so fragmented Most enterprises didn't meticulously design their collaboration stack. They inherited one. Departmental preferences, vendor bundling, and organic employee adoption produced today's environment: Zoom for meetings, Slack or Microsoft Teams for chat, Google Docs or SharePoint for documents, and a growing layer of AI tools that nobody in IT approved. According to BetterCloud's 2026 State of SaaS report, the average organization now deploys 27 AI-powered SaaS applications, making up roughly 22% of its overall software portfolio. The total number of apps per organization grew 11% year over year. And those are just the apps IT knows about. A 2026 Freshworks survey found that 71% of IT leaders acknowledge unapproved AI use is already common across their organizations, even as 92% believe they have full visibility into the tools employees are using. The cost of this fragmentation can go beyond tool sprawl. Decisions made in meetings don't flow into project systems. Chat threads contain context that don't reach the people who need it. Documents live in silos that don't connect to the conversations that produced them. The tools coexist, but they don't connect. They share an org chart, not a data layer. That distinction matters, because it changes what IT actually needs to solve for. Why IT's collaboration mandate looks different now IT used to manage collaboration platforms. Keep them running, keep them patched, keep them licensed. That job still exists, but the surrounding scope has expanded significantly. AI capabilities are commonly embedded inside collaboration platforms, generating content, summarizing conversations, and acting on data in real time. Governance scope now extends to AI-generated outputs, not just stored files. Employees expect seamless movement between meetings, chat, docs, and task management. When those handoffs break, some may route around IT with personal tools and unvetted apps. Security and compliance considerations include how AI processes meeting content, who can access summaries, and where generated data is retained. IT's mandate today is to enable a more governed, integrated collaboration layer where communication, content, and AI share centralized policies and admin controls. That's a fundamentally different scope than managing a set of standalone platforms. And most collaboration environments weren't built to support it. What a modern collaboration environment actually requires A collaboration environment built for the current reality has a few defining characteristics. None of them are about having the most features. All of them are about coherence. The first is a shared governance layer . AI, meetings, chat, docs, and workflows should operate within a shared governance framework that includes centralized admin controls, retention policies, and role-based access controls (RBAC). The second is cross-platform awareness . Enterprises don't run entirely on one vendor. The right collaboration environment acknowledges that and connects to Microsoft 365, Google Workspace, Salesforce, ServiceNow, and the rest of the stack rather than ignoring them. A platform that only accounts for its own ecosystem leaves the majority of your collaboration surface unmanaged. The third is AI that lives inside the collaboration flow . AI capabilities that summarize meetings, compose messages, and capture action items should operate within the same platform employees already use for communication and content creation. When AI use requires a separate product, a standalone IT security review process, and a separate budget line, adoption fragments and governance gaps can widen. The fourth is workflow continuity . Meeting outcomes, chat decisions, and document approvals should be able to trigger downstream actions like task creation, CRM updates, and follow-up scheduling without manual re-entry or context loss. These describe what's possible today. Zoom Workplace was designed to address them, bringing meetings, chat, phone, AI, docs, and workflows together in one governable environment while integrating with the applications organizations already depend on. The question is whether your current environment delivers these capabilities in a coherent way, or whether you're assembling them piecemeal from disconnected tools. Consolidation without the rip-and-replace "Consolidation" can make IT leaders uneasy because it implies migration, disruption, and political battles over entrenched tools. But the version of consolidation that matters here isn't about replacing everything with one vendor. It's about creating a governable center of gravity. Keep the tools that work. Integrate them into a platform that allows for unified governance, a shared AI layer, and centralized admin controls. Consolidate where it reduces complexity, especially around AI, where ungoverned tools can create the most exposure. Many organizations run Microsoft 365, Google Workspace, or both. A collaboration platform that ignores that reality isn't solving the problem. The right platform works alongside those environments and extends AI capabilities across them rather than competing with them. The goal is fewer ungoverned tools, fewer disconnected workflows, and fewer blind spots in how collaboration data moves through the organization. The gaps worth finding now A few questions can reveal how much distance exists between your current collaboration environment and one that was intentionally designed. Do you have visibility into which AI tools employees are using for meeting capture, summarization, and content generation? Can your collaboration environment move meeting outcomes into enterprise systems like your CRM, project management platform, or HR tools without manual re-entry? Are your AI governance policies applied consistently across every collaboration modality, or are they configured tool by tool? And if an employee leaves, do you know where their meeting data, AI-generated content, and chat context lives? These aren't gotcha questions. They're the gaps that separate a collaboration environment that evolved from one that was designed. Closing them starts with understanding where you are today. Zoom Workplace brings meetings, chat, phone, AI, docs, and workflows together in one governable platform, while connecting to the tools your organization already depends on.
